questions.q: In an experiment, participants rated statements as 'true' or 'false.' Statements they had already seen before — regardless of whether the statement was actually true or false — were rated as more likely to be true on a later viewing, simply because they felt more familiar. What is this effect called?
choices: The mere exposure effect: repeated exposure increases liking for a stimulus, not belief in its truth
The illusory truth effect: repeated exposure to a claim increases how true it feels, independent of its actual accuracy
Confirmation bias: people preferentially recall information supporting beliefs they already hold
The halo effect: a positive impression in one area causes positive impressions in unrelated areas

questions.q: Children who already enjoyed drawing for fun were split into two groups. One group was given a reward every time they drew; the other group drew with no reward at all. After the rewards stopped, the previously rewarded group spent noticeably LESS free time drawing than before the experiment — while the unrewarded group's interest held steady. What explains the rewarded group's drop in interest?
choices: Rewards have no measurable effect on intrinsic motivation; the drop was random noise
The overjustification effect: external rewards undermined their original intrinsic motivation
Both groups actually increased their drawing time equally
The unrewarded group secretly practiced more, making the comparison unfair

questions.q: In the 19th century, as steam engines became far more fuel-efficient, each engine needed less coal to produce the same work. Economist William Stanley Jevons observed that this increased efficiency was followed not by a decrease in total coal consumption, but by an increase. What does Jevons paradox describe?
choices: Improvements in the efficiency of using a resource can increase, rather than decrease, that resource's total rate of consumption
Efficiency improvements always proportionally reduce total resource consumption
Coal became more expensive as engines grew efficient, forcing less overall use
The paradox shows that 19th-century efficiency measurements were simply wrong

questions.q: Modern AI can play grandmaster-level chess and solve advanced calculus, yet historically struggled with tasks like folding laundry or walking over uneven terrain — skills a toddler performs easily. Moravec's paradox is the observation that, contrary to intuition, ___.
choices: high-level reasoning requires relatively little computation, while low-level sensorimotor skills require enormous computational resources
toddlers are secretly better at logic and calculus than adults give them credit for
AI will never be able to perform any physical task, no matter how advanced it becomes
computation has no real cost, so the only barrier to any robotic task is better programming

questions.q: In Situation 1, most people choose A: $1,000,000 for certain, over B: a 10% chance of $5,000,000, an 89% chance of $1,000,000, and a 1% chance of nothing. In Situation 2, most people choose D: a 10% chance of $5,000,000 and a 90% chance of nothing, over C: an 11% chance of $1,000,000 and an 89% chance of nothing. Mathematically, switching from A to B is the same reallocation of probability as switching from C to D. What does this Allais paradox demonstrate?
choices: The paradox proves expected-utility theory correctly predicts human choices
$5,000,000 provides no additional utility over $1,000,000, so the two situations are identical
Real human preferences can violate the independence axiom of expected-utility theory, even among people who accept it as rational
People simply made arithmetic errors calculating the probabilities

The statement 'All ravens are black' is logically equivalent to its contrapositive, 'All non-black things are non-ravens.' Hempel's raven paradox asks: does observing a green apple (a non-black, non-raven object) technically count as evidence, however weak, confirming that all ravens are black?
choices: Yes, but only if the apple is unripe
No — only observing an actual raven can ever provide evidence either way
No, because apples and ravens belong to entirely unrelated categories
Yes — by the logic of the contrapositive, it technically counts as extremely weak confirming evidence
